name: Glimepiride
route_note: oral tablet once daily with breakfast
tagline: Once-daily sulfonylurea that stimulates insulin release from beta cells
summary: Glimepiride is a long-acting sulfonylurea taken once daily to lower blood glucose in type 2 diabetes by stimulating insulin secretion. It is widely used, often combined with metformin, and is available as low-cost generics.
mechanism: Glimepiride binds the SUR1 subunit of ATP-sensitive potassium channels in pancreatic beta cells, closing the channels and depolarising the membrane. Calcium influx through voltage-gated channels then triggers insulin secretion.
Its binding kinetics differ from glibenclamide (faster association and dissociation from SUR1), which may partly explain a somewhat lower hypoglycaemia rate in some comparisons.
uses: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, as monotherapy or with metformin, insulin or other agents

history.title: UGDP study
history.detail: The University Group Diabetes Program reports excess cardiovascular mortality with tolbutamide, the origin of the class special warning carried by US sulfonylurea labels.

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: FDA approves Hoechst's Amaryl in November 1995.

history.title: Generic entry
history.detail: Generic glimepiride becomes available in the US.

history.title: CAROLINA trial
history.detail: CAROLINA shows linagliptin non-inferior to glimepiride for cardiovascular outcomes, supporting glimepiride's cardiovascular safety.

history.title: GRADE study
history.detail: The NIH-funded GRADE study compares glimepiride, sitagliptin, liraglutide and glargine added to metformin; glimepiride is intermediate in durability.

pk.metabolism: hepatic CYP2C9 to M1 (active) and M2

safety.boxed_warning: US label carries the class special warning on increased cardiovascular mortality (UGDP study).

facts: In the CAROLINA trial over 6,000 patients were followed for a median 6.3 years.
